source_text: Ecce circumcisus tradit nascenti de se, quo caruit in se. Quid est ergo quod dicis: "Per rerum naturam fieri non posse, ut illud homines probentur tradere, quo caruisse creduntur"? Bonum est praeputium, non est malum, quia Deus illud fecit, sicut de oleastro copiosissime disputasti. … Proinde circumcisio carnis non solum illam quasi generalem sententiam vestram sine ambiguitate subvertit, qua dicitis: "Per rerum naturam fieri non posse, ut quo ipse caruit, tradat proli parens"
pass_a_gloss: Behold, the circumcised hands on to the one being born from him what he lacked in himself. What is it then that you say: 'Through the nature of things it cannot happen that men be proved to hand on that which they are believed to have lacked'? Good is the foreskin, it is not evil, because God made it, as about the wild olive you disputed most copiously. Accordingly the circumcision of the flesh not only overturns without ambiguity that as-it-were general opinion of yours (plural), by which you say: 'Through the nature of things it cannot happen that what he himself lacked, a parent hand on to offspring'.
pass_b_english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “See, the circumcised man hands on to the one born of him what he lacked in himself. What, then, is it that you say: ‘By the nature of things it cannot happen that people should be shown to hand on what they are believed to have lacked’? The foreskin is good, not evil, because God made it, just as you argued at great length about the wild olive.”

“So the circumcision of the flesh not only overturns, beyond doubt, that maxim of yours, general as it were, in which you say: ‘By the nature of things it cannot happen that a parent should hand on to his offspring what he himself lacked’ …”

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

choices.choice: 'quo caruisse creduntur' is 'what they are believed to have lacked', not 'lost' as the old English had it.

2026-11-11 (claude-sumfix2-d): the old English summarised Augustine's report ('Augustine reports that Julian ...') instead of translating it. Now a translation of the Latin clause(s) that carry Julian's words or Augustine's report of them, with Augustine named as speaker where the words are his; nothing added that the Latin does not say. Omitted stretches inside a paragraph are marked with an ellipsis.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Contra Iulianum / Against Julian), including authorities Julian quoted; Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded. This row is Augustine's report; Pass A glosses only the Julian words recoverable here. This row translates Augustine's report addressed to Julian, with Augustine named as speaker; Julian's words are the quoted parts.
